title: Zayin
hook: the letter that begins zachor, remember

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hook of gold, and the little letter that means and. Your line was vav connects. What did you join? Today, a letter that reaches backward. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five.

Here's a puzzle hiding in plain sight. The Ten Commandments appear in the Torah in Exodus, and then again, when Moses retells them, in Deuteronomy. Put the two side by side and they're nearly the same. But the commandment about the Sabbath opens with a different word in each. In Exodus, the first word is zachor: remember. In Deuteronomy, it's shamor: keep, guard, observe. Which one did the people hear at the mountain? The rabbis had an answer, and you can still hear it sung on Friday nights. Today's letter is the first sound of the first one.

Zayin. Four steps into this letter. First, the word it opens. Zachor, remember. In the King James, Exodus says it plainly: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The very first sound of that command is a zayin. So is the first sound of zikaron, a memory, and zecher, a remembrance: other remembering words that open the same way. Second, the other word. Deuteronomy's version opens with shamor, to guard or observe. Remember is something you do inside. Guard is something you do with your hands and your calendar. Two verbs, one day. Third, the rabbis' answer. In the Talmud, in tractate Shevuot, they say God spoke both words at once, in a single utterance, something no human mouth could do. Remember and keep, together. Much later, a poet put that teaching into a song called Lecha Dodi, which congregations sing on Friday evening to welcome the Sabbath. One of its lines says it outright: keep and remember, in one word. So the puzzle became a song. Fourth, why remembering gets its own commandment. In this tradition, memory isn't just what happens to you. It's something you do on purpose. The prayer for the dead said on certain festivals is called Yizkor, may God remember. Zayin turns the past into a task. In a plain week, that might look like this: not waiting for a memory to arrive, but choosing to call someone to mind.
screen: `ZACHOR: REMEMBER THE SABBATH.` · `SHAMOR: GUARD IT.` · `BOTH WORDS, SPOKEN AT ONCE.` · `MEMORY AS SOMETHING YOU DO.` · then, large: `REMEMBER ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember one thing on purpose. Settle, and breathe. Choose something to remember, rather than waiting for it to drift in. A person who taught you something. A morning when things went right. A kindness someone did for you that they've probably forgotten. Bring it back slowly. Where were you? What did it sound like? What did they say? Let the details arrive, one at a time, and stay with them. If you pray, you can hold that memory in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Zayin. The letter that begins zachor, remember, and the family of remembering words: zikaron, zecher, Yizkor. Today's word.
Your line: zayin remembers. Today, tell someone one thing you remembered on purpose, especially if it's about them. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Congregations welcome the Sabbath on Friday evening by singing Lecha Dodi, whose verses include the teaching that 'keep' and 'remember' were spoken as one; the kiddush over wine on Friday night also speaks of the Sabbath as a remembrance.

notes: Exodus 20:8 quoted from the KJV (1769); JPS 1917 reads the same words, but confirm.
Shevuot 20b paraphrased: zachor and shamor were said in a single utterance, which the mouth cannot speak nor the ear hear. Confirm reference and paraphrase.
Lecha Dodi: 'a poet' left unnamed and undated on purpose; 'many congregations sing' it on Friday evening. Confirm.
Yizkor described as 'the prayer for the dead said on certain festivals'. Confirm wording.
Root z-k-r and the words zikaron, zecher are standard lexicon items; confirm.
'Something no human mouth could do' paraphrases the Talmud's point; confirm.
